facts.statement: Brachiosaurus lived during the Late Jurassic period, from the Kimmeridgian to the Tithonian stages.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Late Jurassic (Kimmeridgian to Tithonian),

facts.statement: The genus Brachiosaurus was first described by Elmer S. Riggs in 1903.
facts.quote: parent_authority: Riggs (1903)

facts.statement: Brachiosaurus fossils were first found in the Colorado River valley in western Colorado, United States.
facts.quote: It was first described by American paleontologist Elmer S. Riggs in 1903 from fossils found in the Colorado River valley in western Colorado, United States.

facts.statement: The specific name altithorax means "deep chest", while the generic name Brachiosaurus means "arm lizard" due to its long forelimbs.
facts.quote: Brachiosaurus altithorax; the generic name is Greek for "arm lizard", in reference to its proportionately long arms, and the specific name means "deep chest".

facts.statement: Brachiosaurus is estimated to have been 18 to 22 meters long, with a body mass between 28.3 and 46.9 metric tons.
facts.quote: Brachiosaurus is estimated to have been between 18 and 22 m long; body mass estimates of the subadult holotype specimen range from 28.3 to 46.9 MT.

facts.statement: Brachiosaurus possessed a disproportionately long neck, a small skull, and a large overall size typical of sauropods.
facts.quote: It had a disproportionately long neck, small skull, and large overall size, all of which are typical for sauropods.

facts.statement: While Brachiosaurus was once thought to be ectothermic due to its size, recent research suggests it was warm-blooded.
facts.quote: It has been used as an example of a dinosaur that was most likely ectothermic because of its large size and the corresponding need for sufficient forage, but more recent research suggests it was warm-blooded.

facts.statement: Brachiosaurus is regarded as a high browser capable of reaching vegetation up to 9 meters off the ground.
facts.quote: It is regarded as a high browser, possibly cropping or nipping vegetation as high as 9 m off the ground.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen comes from the Brushy Basin Member of the Morrison Formation and dates to about 154 to 153 million years ago.
facts.quote: This specimen, which was later declared the holotype, comes from rocks of the Brushy Basin Member of the Morrison Formation, and therefore is late Kimmeridgian in age, about 154to 153million years old.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen was discovered by Elmer S. Riggs and his crew from the Field Columbian Museum and is cataloged as FMNHP25107.
facts.quote: Discovered by American paleontologist Elmer S. Riggs and his crew from the Field Columbian Museum (now the Field Museum of Natural History) of Chicago, it is currently cataloged as FMNHP25107.

facts.statement: Elmer S. Riggs initially mistook the holotype for a badly preserved Brontosaurus and prioritized excavating a Morosaurus skeleton first.
facts.quote: Riggs at first took the find for a badly preserved Brontosaurus specimen and gave priority to excavating Quarry 12, which held a more promising Morosaurus skeleton.

facts.statement: Riggs initially misidentified the holotype humerus as a deformed femur, a mistake confirmed by the discovery of a real femur of similar size.
facts.quote: During excavation of the specimen, Riggs misidentified the humerus as a deformed femur due to its great length, and this seemed to be confirmed when an equally-sized, well-preserved real femur of the same skeleton was discovered.

facts.statement: The holotype skeleton includes the right humerus, femur, ilium, coracoid, sacrum, seven thoracic vertebrae, two caudal vertebrae, and several ribs.
facts.quote: The holotype skeleton consists of the right humerus (upper arm bone), the right femur (thigh bone), the right ilium (a hip bone), the right coracoid (a shoulder bone), the sacrum (fused vertebrae of the hip), the last seven thoracic (trunk) and two caudal (tail) vertebrae, and several ribs.

facts.statement: Although Riggs originally described the coracoid as left-sided, restudy confirmed it is from the right side of the body.
facts.quote: Riggs described the coracoid as from the left side of the body, but restudy has shown it to be a right coracoid.

facts.statement: A Brachiosaurus skull was discovered in 1883 by farmer Marshall Parker Felch near Garden Park, Colorado.
facts.quote: In 1883, farmer Marshall Parker Felch, a fossil collector for the American paleontologist Othniel Charles Marsh, reported the discovery of a sauropod skull in Felch Quarry 1, near Garden Park, Colorado.

facts.statement: The skull was found near a 1-meter-long cervical vertebra that was destroyed while being collected.
facts.quote: The skull was found in yellowish white sandstone, near a 1 m cervical vertebra, which was destroyed during an attempt to collect it.

facts.statement: The skull was sent to the National Museum of Natural History in 1899 and cataloged as USNM 5730.
facts.quote: Most of the specimens collected by Felch were sent to the National Museum of Natural History in 1899 after Marsh's death, including the skull, which was then cataloged as USNM 5730.

facts.statement: A shoulder blade and coracoid from Dry Mesa Quarry, Colorado, were central to the Supersaurus and Ultrasauros debate in the 1980s and 1990s.
facts.quote: A shoulder blade with coracoid from Dry Mesa Quarry, Colorado, is one of the specimens at the center of the Supersaurus/Ultrasauros issue of the 1980s and 1990s.

facts.statement: In 2009, Michael P. Taylor concluded that the Dry Mesa shoulder blade could not be referred to B. altithorax.
facts.quote: in 2009 Michael P. Taylor concluded that it could not be referred to B. altithorax.

facts.statement: The Dry Mesa 'ultrasaur' was found to be smaller than Riggs's original Brachiosaurus specimen based on coracoid dimensions.
facts.quote: The Dry Mesa "ultrasaur" was not as large as had been thought; the dimensions of the shoulder's coracoid bone indicate that the animal was smaller than Riggs's original specimen of Brachiosaurus.

facts.statement: Large-scale expeditions in German East Africa discovered significant brachiosaurid fossils in the Tendaguru Formation between 1909 and 1912.
facts.quote: Between 1909 and 1912, large-scale paleontological expeditions in German East Africa unearthed a considerable amount of brachiosaurid material from the Tendaguru Formation.

facts.statement: German paleontologist Werner Janensch described the Tendaguru fossils as belonging to the genus Brachiosaurus in 1914.
facts.quote: In 1914, German paleontologist Werner Janensch listed differences and commonalities between these fossils and B. altithorax, concluding they could be referred to the genus Brachiosaurus.

facts.statement: Werner Janensch named two species from the Tendaguru material: the larger Brachiosaurus brancai and the smaller Brachiosaurus fraasi.
facts.quote: From this material Janensch named two species: Brachiosaurus brancai for the larger and more complete taxon, and Brachiosaurus fraasi for the smaller and more poorly known species.

facts.statement: A nearly complete Brachiosaurus skeleton was collected by F.W.H. Migeod for the British Museum of Natural History in 1930.
facts.quote: Additional material was collected by the British Museum of Natural History's Tendaguru expedition, including a nearly complete skeleton (BMNH R5937) collected by F.W.H. Migeod in 1930.

facts.statement: Werner Janensch originally described Brachiosaurus brancai based on a skeleton that he later found consisted of two partial individuals.
facts.quote: Janensch based his description of B. brancai on "Skelett S" (skeleton S) from Tendaguru, but later realized that it comprised two partial individuals: SI and SII.

facts.statement: The lectotype specimen of Brachiosaurus brancai includes dorsal vertebrae, shoulder girdle elements, forelimb bones, hands, pelvic bones, and hindlimb bones.
facts.quote: It includes, among other bones, several dorsal vertebrae, the left scapula, both coracoids, the breastbones, both humeri, both ulnae and radii (lower arm bones), a right hand, a partial left hand, both hip bones and the right femur, tibia and fibula (shank bones).

facts.statement: The name Giraffatitan was elevated to full genus status by George Olshevsky in 1991 based on differences in vertebral variation.
facts.quote: Giraffatitan was raised to full genus level by George Olshevsky in 1991, while referring to the vertebral variation.

facts.statement: While Daniel Chure rejected the separation of the African material in 2010, most subsequent studies from 2012 onward have accepted it as the genus Giraffatitan.
facts.quote: The split was rejected by Daniel Chure in 2010, but from 2012 onward most studies recognized the name Giraffatitan.

facts.statement: Brachiosaurid remains were discovered in 1947 at Atalaia, Portugal, within rock layers dating to the Tithonian stage.
facts.quote: In 1947, at Atalaia in Portugal, brachiosaurid remains were found in layers dating from the Tithonian.

facts.statement: Albert-Félix de Lapparent and Georges Zbyszewski named the Portuguese fossils Brachiosaurus atalaiensis in 1957.
facts.quote: Albert-Félix de Lapparent and Georges Zbyszewski named them as the species Brachiosaurus atalaiensis in 1957.

facts.statement: Miguel Telles Antunes and Octávio Mateus transferred Brachiosaurus atalaiensis to its own genus, Lusotitan, in 2003.
facts.quote: Shortly before the publication of the 2004 book, the species had been placed in its own genus Lusotitan by Miguel Telles Antunes and Octávio Mateus in 2003.

facts.statement: The lectotype for Lusotitan consists of a partial postcranial skeleton containing twenty-eight vertebrae, ribs, shoulder elements, forelimb bones, pelvic fragments, and hindlimb bones.
facts.quote: Antunes and Mateus selected a partial postcranial skeleton (MIGM4978, 4798, 4801–4810, 4938, 4944, 4950, 4952, 4958, 4964–4966, 4981–4982, 4985, 8807, 8793–87934) as the lectotype; this specimen includes twenty-eight vertebrae, chevrons, ribs, a possible shoulder blade, humeri, forearm bones, partial left pelvis, lower leg bones, and part of the right ankle.

facts.statement: French geologist F. Nougarède reported finding fragmentary brachiosaurid remains in the Sahara Desert of eastern Algeria in 1958.
facts.quote: In 1958 French petroleum geologist F. Nougarède reported to have discovered fragmentary brachiosaurid remains in eastern Algeria, in the Sahara Desert.

facts.statement: Albert-Félix de Lapparent described and named the species Brachiosaurus nougaredi in 1960 based on the Algerian fossils.
facts.quote: Based on these, Albert-Félix de Lapparent described and named the species Brachiosaurus nougaredi in 1960.

facts.statement: Albert-Félix de Lapparent assigned the rock layers to the Late Jurassic age partly because he believed Brachiosaurus fossils were present.
facts.quote: He assigned the rocks to this age in part because of the presumed presence of Brachiosaurus.

facts.statement: Recent reviews have placed the rock layer containing these fossils in the Albian age of the Early Cretaceous, making them significantly younger than originally thought.
facts.quote: A more recent review placed it in the "Continental intercalaire", which is considered to belong to the Albian age of the late Early Cretaceous, significantly younger.

facts.statement: The type material for Brachiosaurus nougaredi consists of a weathered sacrum and fragments of left hand bones found at the discovery site.
facts.quote: The type material moved to Paris consisted of a sacrum, weathered out at the desert surface, and some of the left metacarpals and phalanges.

facts.statement: Later analysis concluded the hand bones belonged to an indeterminate titanosauriform, and the sacrum was reported lost in 2013.
facts.quote: The metacarpals were concluded to belong to some indeterminate titanosauriform. The sacrum was reported lost in 2013.

facts.statement: Only four of the five sacral vertebrae are preserved, and the original sacrum was estimated at 1.3 meters long in 1960, larger than the 0.91-meter sacrum of B. altithorax.
facts.quote: Only four out of the five sacral vertebrae are preserved. The total original length was in 1960 estimated at 1.3 m, compared to 0.91 m with B. altithorax.

facts.statement: The estimated size of the Brachiosaurus nougaredi sacrum makes it the largest known sauropod sacrum, aside from those of Argentinosaurus and Apatosaurus.
facts.quote: This would make it larger than any other sauropod sacrum ever found, except those of Argentinosaurus and Apatosaurus.

facts.statement: Size estimates for Brachiosaurus altithorax are largely based on the more complete remains of the related genus Giraffatitan.
facts.quote: Most estimates of Brachiosaurus altithorax size are based on the related brachiosaurid Giraffatitan (formerly known as B. brancai), which is known from much more complete material than Brachiosaurus.

facts.statement: The size of the North American Brachiosaurus is uncertain because its most complete specimen appears to be a subadult, indicated by an unfused suture between the coracoid and scapula.
facts.quote: There is another element of uncertainty for the North American Brachiosaurus because the type (and most complete) specimen appears to represent a subadult, as indicated by the unfused suture between the coracoid, a bone of the shoulder girdle that forms part of the shoulder joint, and the scapula (shoulder blade).

facts.statement: The mass of the holotype Brachiosaurus specimen has been estimated to range from 28.3 to 46.9 metric tons.
facts.quote: Over the years, the mass of the holotype specimen has been estimated within the range of 28.3 - 46.9 MT.

facts.statement: Brachiosaurus has been estimated to reach lengths of 18 to 22 meters and heights of 9.4 to 13 meters.
facts.quote: The length of Brachiosaurus has been estimated at 20–22 meters (66–72ft) and 18 m, and its height at 9.4 m and 12 - 13 m.

facts.statement: The most complete Giraffatitan skeleton likely does not represent the maximum size of the genus, as another fibula is thirteen percent longer.
facts.quote: As with the main Brachiosaurus specimen, Giraffatitan specimen MB.R.2181 likely does not reflect the maximum size of the genus, as a fibula (specimen HMXV2) is thirteen percent longer than that of MB.R.2181.

facts.statement: Brachiosaurus was a quadrupedal dinosaur characterized by a small skull, long neck, large trunk, muscular tail, and slender columnar limbs.
facts.quote: Like all sauropod dinosaurs, Brachiosaurus was a quadruped with a small skull, a long neck, a large trunk with a high-ellipsoid cross section, a long, muscular tail and slender, columnar limbs.

facts.statement: Although the neck is missing from the holotype, related species like Giraffatitan possessed a very long neck consisting of thirteen elongated cervical vertebrae.
facts.quote: The neck is not preserved in the holotype specimen, but was very long even by sauropod standards in the closely related Giraffatitan, consisting of thirteen elongated cervical (neck) vertebrae.

facts.statement: The neck was held in a slight S-curve with bent lower and upper sections and a straight middle section.
facts.quote: The neck was held in a slight S-curve, with the lower and upper sections bent and a straight middle section.

facts.statement: Brachiosaurus likely possessed very elongated neck ribs that ran down the underside of the neck and overlapped several preceding vertebrae.
facts.quote: Brachiosaurus likely shared with Giraffatitan the very elongated neck ribs, which ran down the underside of the neck, overlapping several preceding vertebrae.

facts.statement: The broadened neural spine on the single discovered tail vertebra indicates the tail was possibly 20 to 25 percent longer than in Giraffatitan.
facts.quote: This vertebra had a much greater area for ligament attachment due to a broadened neural spine, indicating that the tail was also longer than in Giraffatitan, possibly by 20 to 25 percent.

facts.statement: The preserved humerus measures 204 cm in length, with an estimated original length of 216 cm after accounting for erosion.
facts.quote: The humerus, as preserved, measures 204 cm in length, though part of its lower end was lost to erosion; its original length is estimated at 216 cm.

facts.statement: There is a debate regarding neck length, with Gregory S. Paul suggesting it was shorter than Giraffatitan's in 1988, while Mike P. Taylor argued in 2009 that vertebrae proportions indicated otherwise.
facts.quote: In 1988, paleontologist Gregory S. Paul suggested that the neck of Brachiosaurus was shorter than that of Giraffatitan, but in 2009, paleontologist Mike P. Taylor pointed out that two cervical vertebrae likely belonging to Brachiosaurus had identical proportions.

facts.statement: Researchers D'Emic and Carrano estimated the Brachiosaurus skull to be 70 centimeters long, 55 centimeters tall, and 35 centimeters wide.
facts.quote: D'Emic and Carrano instead estimated the skull to have been 70 cm long, and if proportionally similar to that of Giraffatitan, about 55 cm tall, and 35 cm wide

facts.statement: The Brachiosaurus premaxilla was longer than that of Camarasaurus, creating a very long snout.
facts.quote: The premaxilla appears to have been longer than that of Camarasaurus, sloping more gradually toward the nasal bar, which created the very long snout

facts.statement: Each maxilla of Brachiosaurus held space for fourteen or fifteen teeth, more than the eleven found in Giraffatitan or the eight to ten in Camarasaurus.
facts.quote: Each maxilla had space for fourteen or fifteen teeth, whereas Giraffatitan had eleven and Camarasaurus eight to ten

facts.statement: Brachiosaurus teeth exhibited a high degree of dental complexity compared to other sauropods.
facts.quote: The teeth of Brachiosaurus exhibited a high degree of dental complexity relative to other sauropods

facts.statement: The interdental plates in the Brachiosaurus maxilla were thin, fused, porous, and triangular in shape.
facts.quote: The interdental plates of the maxilla were thin, fused, porous, and triangular

facts.statement: A 1997 study by Leonardo Salgado suggested that Brachiosaurus and related genera were not a separate branch but offshoots of the Titanosauriformes stem group.
facts.quote: In 1997, he published an analysis in which species traditionally considered brachiosaurids were subsequent offshoots of the stem of a larger grouping, the Titanosauriformes, and not a separate branch of their own.

facts.statement: In 2009, Taylor reclassified Brachiosaurus brancai as the separate genus Giraffatitan based on multiple anatomical differences.
facts.quote: In 2009, Taylor noted multiple anatomical differences between the two Brachiosaurus species, and consequently moved B. brancai into its own genus, Giraffatitan.

facts.statement: Brachiosaurus was adapted for a terrestrial lifestyle with slender limbs, a high chest, wide hips, high ilia, and a short tail.
facts.quote: Brachiosaurus would have been better adapted than other sauropods to a fully terrestrial lifestyle through its slender limbs, high chest, wide hips, high ilia and short tail.

facts.statement: In 1990, Stephen Czerkas hypothesized that Brachiosaurus occasionally entered water to thermoregulate.
facts.quote: In 1990 the paleontologist Stephen Czerkas stated that Brachiosaurus could have entered water occasionally to cool off (thermoregulate).

facts.statement: There is an ongoing debate about whether the neck posture of Brachiosaurus was near-vertical or horizontal.
facts.quote: Ongoing debate revolves around the neck posture of brachiosaurids, with estimates ranging from near-vertical to horizontal orientations.

facts.statement: In 1999, Olivier Rieppel and Christopher Brochu defended the near-vertical neck posture of Brachiosaurus, citing its long forelimbs and upward-sloping backbone.
facts.quote: Museum paleontologists Olivier Rieppel and Christopher Brochu defended the posture in 1999, noting the long forelimbs and upward sloping backbone.

facts.statement: In 2001, Gunga and Kirsch concluded that Brachiosaurus moved its neck laterally more often than vertically while feeding.
facts.quote: In studying the inner ear of Giraffatitan, Gunga & Kirsch (2001) concluded that brachiosaurids would have moved their necks in lateral directions more often than in dorsal-ventral directions while feeding.

facts.statement: Brachiosaurus likely ate ginkgos, conifers, tree ferns, and large cycads, consuming an estimated 200 to 400 kilograms of plant matter daily.
facts.quote: Its diet likely consisted of ginkgos, conifers, tree ferns, and large cycads, with intake estimated at 200 to 400 kg of plant matter daily in a 2007 study.

facts.statement: Brachiosaurus fed using a simple up-and-down jaw motion.
facts.quote: Brachiosaurid feeding involved simple up-and-down jaw motion.

facts.statement: Brachiosaurus could reach a height of over 9 meters above the ground even with a less inclined neck.
facts.quote: Even if it did not hold its neck near vertical, and instead had a less inclined neck, its head height may still have been over 9 m above the ground.

facts.statement: Brachiosaurus probably fed mostly on foliage located above 5 meters.
facts.quote: It probably fed mostly on foliage above 5 m.

facts.statement: If feeding for sixteen hours a day, Brachiosaurus would have taken between one and six bites per minute, consuming roughly 1.5 percent of its body mass daily.
facts.quote: If it fed sixteen hours per day, biting off between a tenth and two-thirds of a kilogram, taking between one and six bites per minute, its daily food intake would have equaled roughly 1.5 percent of its body mass, comparable to the requirement of a modern elephant.

facts.statement: Brachiosaurus had shorter arms and lower shoulders, making it less adapted to high-browsing than Giraffatitan.
facts.quote: Brachiosaurus, with its shorter arms and lower shoulders, was not as well-adapted to high-browsing as Giraffatitan.

facts.statement: In 2016, Hallett and Wedel rejected the hypothesis that Brachiosaurus nostrils were at the snout tip, suggesting they were placed at the top of the head as traditionally thought.
facts.quote: Hallett and Wedel therefore in 2016 rejected his interpretation and suggested that they were in fact placed at the top of the head, above the bony nostrils, as traditionally thought.

facts.statement: In 2001, Lawrence M. Witmer argued that the fleshy nostrils of Brachiosaurus were likely placed at the front of the bony opening, similar to modern land animals.
facts.quote: The American paleontologist Lawrence M. Witmer rejected this reconstruction in 2001, pointing out that all living vertebrate land animals have their external fleshy nostrils placed at the front of the bony nostril.

facts.statement: Czerkas speculated that the large nasal opening of Brachiosaurus may have housed tissue for enhanced smelling, noting that the exact location of the nostrils remains inconclusive without skin impressions.
facts.quote: Czerkas speculated on the function of the peculiar brachiosaurid nose, and pointed out that there was no conclusive way to determine where the nostrils where located, unless a head with skin impressions was found.

facts.statement: It has been proposed that Brachiosaurus may have had a proboscis to increase upward reach, though this is disputed by some researchers.
facts.quote: It has been proposed that sauropods, including Brachiosaurus, may have had proboscises (trunks) based on the position of the bony narial orifice, to increase their upward reach.

facts.statement: Russel (1989) argued that endothermy was unlikely for Brachiosaurus due to the combination of its great size and high caloric needs.
facts.quote: Russel (1989) used Brachiosaurus as an example of a dinosaur for which endothermy is unlikely, because of the combination of great size (leading to overheating) and great caloric needs to fuel endothermy.

facts.statement: Brachiosaurus used a bird-like respiratory system with air sacs to achieve unidirectional airflow in its lungs.
facts.quote: The respiration system of sauropods, like that of birds, made use of air sacs.

facts.statement: Air sacs in Brachiosaurus connected to the skeleton via pneumatic openings that hollowed out many bones to lighten the weight.
facts.quote: by means of air channels they were connected to much of the skeleton. These branches, the diverticula, via pneumatic openings invaded many bones and strongly hollowed them out.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest the hollowed bones from air sacs may have helped Brachiosaurus remove excess heat for thermoregulation.
facts.quote: They might also have removed excess heat to aid thermoregulation.

facts.statement: In 2012, Carballido and colleagues reconstructed the growth of Brachiosaurus using a 2-meter-long juvenile skeleton named Toni.
facts.quote: The ontogeny of Brachiosaurus has been reconstructed by Carballido and colleagues in 2012 based on Toni (SMA 0009), a postcranial skeleton of a young juvenile with an estimated total body length of just 2 m.

facts.statement: The juvenile Brachiosaurus had middle neck vertebrae that were 1.8 times longer than high, whereas the adult Giraffatitan had a ratio of 4.5.
facts.quote: The middle neck vertebrae of SMA 0009 are remarkably short for a sauropod, being just 1.8 times longer than high, compared with a ratio of 4.5 in Giraffatitan.

facts.statement: The juvenile Brachiosaurus had a metacarpal-to-radius ratio of 0.33, the lowest known among all Neosauropods.
facts.quote: Brachiosaurus also appears to have experienced an elongation of the metacarpals, which in juveniles were shorter compared to the length of the radius; SMA 0009 had a ratio of just 0.33, the lowest known in the entire Neosauropoda.

facts.statement: It is debated whether the juvenile skeleton Toni belongs to Brachiosaurus altithorax or represents a new species due to unique traits and differences from the adult holotype.
facts.quote: These commonalities include an elevation on the rear blade of the ilium; the lack of a postspinal lamina; vertical neural spines on the back; an ilium with a subtle notch between the appendage for the ischium and the rear blade; and the lack of a side bulge on the upper thighbone. There are also differences; these might indicate that the juvenile is not a B. altithorax individual after all, but belongs to a new species.

facts.statement: Brachiosaurus lived during the Kimmeridgian and Tithonian ages, between 155.6 and 145.5 million years ago.
facts.quote: from the Kimmeridgian and Tithonian ages (155.6 to 145.5 million years ago)

facts.statement: Brachiosaurus was first described by Elmer S. Riggs in 1903.
facts.quote: Fue descrita por primera vez por Elmer S. Riggs en 1903

facts.statement: The fossils used to describe Brachiosaurus were found in the Grand Canyon river, now the Colorado River in western Colorado, within the Morrison Formation of the United States.
facts.quote: a partir de fósiles encontrados en el río del Gran Cañón, ahora Río Colorado del oeste de Colorado, en sedimentos de la famosa Formación Morrison, Estados Unidos

facts.statement: Brachiosaurus is characterized by an extremely long neck, a small skull, and a large overall size.
facts.quote: Brachiosaurus tiene el cuello extremadamente largo, un cráneo pequeño y gran tamaño general

facts.statement: Brachiosaurus had front legs that were longer than its hind legs.
facts.quote: siendo las patas delanteras más largas que las patas traseras

facts.statement: The Brachiosaurus skull featured a wide, robust snout, a large jaw, and spatulate-shaped teeth.
facts.quote: El cráneo tenía un hocico ancho y robusto y con una gran mandíbula, con dientes en forma de espátula

facts.statement: Brachiosaurus possessed large air sacs connected to its lungs in the neck and trunk, including vertebrae and ribs, which significantly reduced its weight.
facts.quote: Tenía grandes sacos de aire conectados al sistema pulmonar que estaban presentes en el cuello y el tronco, incluyendo las vértebras y costillas, reduciendo en gran medida el peso

facts.statement: Unlike most sauropods, Brachiosaurus had forelimbs that were longer than its hind limbs.
facts.quote: Inusualmente para un saurópodo, las extremidades anteriores eran más largas que las extremidades traseras

facts.statement: The femur of the type specimen of Brachiosaurus measured only 2.03 meters in length.
facts.quote: El fémur, hueso del muslo, del espécimen tipo mide solamente 2,03 metros de largo

facts.statement: Unlike other sauropods, Brachiosaurus appears to have had a slightly depressed shoulder joint and an unusually deep ribcage.
facts.quote: A diferencia de otros saurópodos, Brachiosaurus parece haber tenido ligeramente tumbada la articulación del hombro, y la caja torácica era inusualmente profunda

facts.statement: The deep ribcage and shoulder structure caused Brachiosaurus's trunk to be inclined, with the front much higher than the hips.
facts.quote: Esto hacía que el tronco estuviese inclinado, con la parte delantera mucho más alta que las caderas

facts.statement: In general, Brachiosaurus's body shape resembles a giraffe more than any other living animal.
facts.quote: En general, esta forma se asemeja a una jirafa más que cualquier otro animal vivo

facts.statement: Brachiosaurus is considered a high browser that likely nibbled vegetation from tree canopies possibly as high as 9 meters above the ground.
facts.quote: Brachiosaurus es considerado como un alto ramoneador, que probablemente hubiese mordisqueado o pellizcado la vegetación de la copa de los árboles posiblemente tan alto como 9 metros por encima del suelo

facts.statement: While once thought to be ectothermic due to its size and feeding needs, recent research indicates Brachiosaurus was likely endothermic (warm-blooded).
facts.quote: Brachiosaurus se ha utilizado como un ejemplo de un dinosaurio que era probablemente ectotérmico debido a su gran tamaño y su necesidad de alimentación, pero investigaciones más recientes han demostrado que habría sido de sangre caliente

facts.statement: The estimated length of Brachiosaurus is 26 meters.
facts.quote: La longitud del Brachiosaurus se ha estimado en 26 metros

facts.statement: Estimates for the mass of B. altithorax range from 35.0 tons (Paul, 1988) to 56.3 metric tons (Benson, 2014), with intermediate estimates of 43.9 tons (Foster, 2003) and 28.7 tons (Taylor, 2009).
facts.quote: la masa de B. altithorax se ha estimado en 35,0 toneladas por Paul en 1988, 43,9 toneladas por Foster en 2003, 28,7 toneladas por Taylor en 2009 y, más recientemente, en 56,3 toneladas métricas por Benson en 2014

facts.statement: Brachiosaurus belongs to the family Brachiosauridae.
facts.quote: familia: Brachiosauridae

facts.quote: genus_authority: Riggs, 1903

facts.statement: The species B. altithorax was described by Riggs in 1903.
facts.quote: species_authority: Riggs, 1903

facts.statement: Much of what is known about Brachiosaurus is based on Giraffatitan brancai, originally described by Werner Janensch as a Brachiosaurus species in 1914, though it is now considered a separate genus.
facts.quote: Gran parte de lo que se conoce sobre Brachiosaurus se basa de hecho en Giraffatitan brancai, una especie de dinosaurio braquiosáurido de la Formación Tendaguru de Tanzania que fue descrito originalmente por el paleontólogo alemán Werner Janensch como una especie de Brachiosaurus en 1914

facts.statement: Brachiosaurus was one of the less abundant sauropods in the Morrison Formation.
facts.quote: Brachiosaurus was one of the less abundant Morrison Formation sauropods

facts.statement: A 2003 survey by John Foster reported 12 specimens of the genus Brachiosaurus among more than two hundred fossil localities.

facts.statement: It is debated whether much or all of the material attributed to Brachiosaurus actually belongs to Giraffatitan, though some may represent a new brachiosaurid.
facts.quote: Mucho o todo este material pertenece probablemente a Giraffatitan, aunque algunos pueden representar un nuevo braquiosáurido

facts.statement: The holotype for the genus Brachiosaurus and the species B. altithorax is the fossil specimen FMNH 25107.
facts.quote: FMNH 25107 es el holotipo tanto del género Brachiosaurus como de la especie B. altithorax

facts.statement: Elmer Riggs originally described the coracoid bone of the holotype as being on the left side, but later studies placed it on the right.
facts.quote: Riggs describe al coracoides a la izquierda del cuerpo, pero posteriores estudios lo colocan a la derecha

facts.statement: In 1969, a study by Kingham moved B. altithorax and several other species into the genus Astrodon, a classification that was not widely accepted.
facts.quote: En 1969, durante un estudio de Kingham, Brachiosaurus altithorax, junto con especies asignadas ahora a otros géneros, se movieron del género

facts.statement: The genus Brachiosaurus is the eponym for the family Brachiosauridae, which takes its name from the genus.
facts.quote: Brachiosaurus es el género epónimo de Brachiosauridae, familia a la que le da nombre

facts.statement: The family Brachiosauridae is located at the base of the Titanosauriformes group, which also includes titanosaurs.
facts.quote: Brachiosauridae está situada en la base de Titanosauriformes, un grupo de saurópodos, que también incluye a los titanosaurios

facts.statement: According to a revised diagnosis by Taylor, B. altithorax is defined by a plethora of distinctive traits, many of which are found on the posterior dorsal vertebrae.
facts.quote: De acuerdo con el diagnóstico revisado por Taylor, Brachiosaurus altithorax se diagnostica como una plétora de rasgos distintivos muchos de los cuales se encuentran en la parte posterior de las vértebras dorsales

facts.statement: A key diagnostic trait placing the animal in Brachiosauridae is a humerus-to-femur length ratio of at least 0.9.
facts.quote: Entre los rasgos distintivos que lo colocan en la familia Brachiosauridae son una relación entre la longitud del húmero al fémur longitud de al menos 0,9

facts.statement: Another diagnostic feature is a very flattened femoral shaft with a ratio of at least 1.85.
facts.quote: y un eje del fémur es muy aplanada (relación ≥1.85)

facts.statement: Walter Janensch based his description of B. brancai on the "Skeleton S" from the Tendaguru Formation, which he later realized consisted of two partial individuals, S I and S II.
facts.quote: Janensch baso su descripción en el "Esqueleto S" de laformación Tendaguru, pero más tarde se dio cuenta de que comprendía dos individuos parciales: S I y S II

facts.statement: Janensch originally did not designate a syntype series but selected S I (MB.R.2180) as the lectotype in 1935.
facts.quote: Él al principio no los designó como una serie sintipo, pero en 1935 hizo S I, MB.R.2180, el lectotipo

facts.statement: In 2009, Michael Taylor proposed the larger and more complete S II (MB.R.2181) as the lectotype, unaware that Janensch had already designated S I.
facts.quote: Taylor en 2009, sin darse cuenta de esta acción, propuso el más grande y más completo S II, MB.R.2181, como el lectotipo

facts.statement: A re-evaluation of the relationship between African and American brachiosaurid material suggests a separate generic name is justified for the Tendaguru material, leading to the transfer of "B. brancai" to the genus Giraffatitan.
facts.quote: Una revaluación de la relación entre el material de braquiosáurido africano y americano indica que un nombre genérico separado está justificado para el material de Tendaguru, por lo que "B. brancai" se ha trasladado a su propio género Giraffatitan

facts.statement: Brachiosaurus is typically viewed as a high browser, feeding on foliage in the tree canopy rather than on the ground.
facts.quote: A Brachiosaurus se lo suele ver como un folívoro alto, alimentándose en el follaje en las copas de los árboles más que sobre la tierra

facts.statement: Even with a straight neck rather than one held vertically, the animal's head height could have exceeded 9 meters above the ground.
facts.quote: Incluso si no tenía el cuello cerca de la vertical, y en su lugar tenía un cuello recto, su altura de la cabeza puede haber estado a más de 9 metros sobre el suelo

facts.statement: Its diet likely consisted of ginkgos, conifers, tree ferns, and large cycads, with an estimated daily consumption of 200 to 400 kilograms of plant matter.
facts.quote: Su dieta consistía probablemente en ginkgos, coníferas, helechos arborescentes y cicadáceas grandes, con un consumo estimado en 200 a 400 kilogramos de materia vegetal diariamente

facts.statement: Feeding in Brachiosaurus involved a simple up-and-down movement of the jaw.
facts.quote: La alimentación del Brachiosaurus implicaba un simple movimiento de la mandíbula hacia arriba y hacia abajo

facts.statement: The teeth were arranged to cut material as they closed and were likely used for raking or cutting vegetation.
facts.quote: Los dientes se dispusieron para cortar el material a medida que se cerraban, y probablemente se usaron para rastrillar y/o cortar la vegetación

facts.statement: It has been repeatedly suggested, for example in the movie Jurassic Park, that Brachiosaurus could adopt a bipedal or tripod stance with tail support to feed.
facts.quote: Se ha sugerido repetidamente, por ejemplo, en la película Jurassic Park, que Brachiosaurus podría adoptar una posición bípeda o trípode, con soporte de cola, para alimentarse

facts.statement: However, a detailed physical modeling analysis by Heinrich Mallison showed that while many sauropods could stand on their hind legs, the body shape and exceptionally long forelimbs of Brachiosaurus would have made this unlikely.
facts.quote: Sin embargo, un análisis basado en el modelado físico detallado de las capacidades de los saurópodos de Heinrich Mallison mostró que mientras muchos saurópodos podrían levantarse sobre sus patas traseras, la relación de la forma del cuerpo del Brachiosaurus y la longitud del miembro anterior excepcionalmente larga habría hecho poco probable el poder hacerlo

facts.statement: Brachiosaurus would have gained relatively little by standing up, only 33% more feeding height, compared to other sauropods for which a bipedal posture could have tripled feeding height.
facts.quote: Brachiosaurus también habría ganado relativamente poco con levantarse, sólo el 33% más de altura de alimentación, en comparación con otros saurópodos, para los cuales una postura bípeda puede haber triplicado la altura de alimentación

facts.statement: A major difference between the two genera is the general body shape, with Brachiosaurus having a trunk 23% longer and a tail 20 to 25% longer and also higher.
facts.quote: Una diferencia importante entre los dos géneros es la forma general del cuerpo, con Brachiosaurus teniendo un tronco 23% más largo y una cola 20 a 25% más larga y también más alta

facts.statement: De Lapparent and Zbyszewski described a series of remains for "B." atalaiensis but did not designate a type specimen.

facts.statement: Antunes and Mateus selected a partial postcranial skeleton, including specimens MIGM 4978, 4798, and others, as the lectotype for Lusotitan.

facts.statement: Low neural spines, a prominent deltopectoral crest on the humerus, a muscle insertion site on the arm bone, a long and slender humerus, and a long iliac shaft inclined upward indicate that Lusotitan is a brachiosaurid.
facts.quote: Las espinas neurales bajas, la cresta deltopectoral prominente del húmero, un sitio de inserción muscular en el hueso del brazo, el húmero alargado muy largo y esbelto y el eje largo del ilion inclinado hacia arriba indican que Lusotitan es un braquiosáurido
